column4: This ayah itself places الْمَيْسِرِ, the y-s-r family's gambling sense developed in the source, beside the question of what to spend; قُلِ الْعَفْوَ turns an accidental gaming share into a deliberate surplus given away.

وَأَن تَسْتَقْسِمُوا بِالْأَزْلَامِ directly names seeking a share by arrows, while الْمُتَرَدِّيَةُ in the same ayah recalls the source's تَرَدَّى scene; both the lot and the fallen carcass are placed under divine prohibition rather than chance ownership.
الْمَيْسِرُ and الْأَزْلَامُ name both the game and its arrows, and فَاجْتَنِبُوهُ uses the j-n-b family echoed by the God-fearing giver being kept away from the fire in 92:17.
وَمَا لَهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ مِنْ خَلَاقٍ uses خَلَاق in the source's dictionary sense of an allotted share: asking only for the nearer world leaves no share in the last.
لَا خَلَاقَ لَهُمْ فِي الْآخِرَةِ makes the sold covenant yield no final share, and وَلَا يُزَكِّيهِمْ reverses the giver's self-purification in 92:18.
أَمْ لِلْإِنسَانِ مَا تَمَنَّى denies that a person's wish creates a possession or allotted outcome, exposing the false premise behind relying on a lucky arrow.
فَلِلَّهِ الْآخِرَةُ وَالْأُولَى is the exact ownership claim of 92:13 and locates both the first and last with the one who measures the share.
Spend from what God جَعَلَكُم مُّسْتَخْلَفِينَ فِيهِ: the giver can call wealth his, yet holds it as a successor, which makes divine ownership the ground of giving.
The ayah condemns withholding what God gave and ends وَلِلَّهِ مِيرَاثُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ; hoarded wealth finally returns to its actual owner.
لَهُ الْحَمْدُ فِي الْأُولَى وَالْآخِرَةِ joins divine possession of first and last to praise, and its closing judgment and return explain what that ownership entails.
وَلَلْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لَّكَ مِنَ الْأُولَى gives the first and last a value-order for the Prophet, while 92:13 states whose they are.
سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى repeats the source's joined title رَبِّهِ الْأَعْلَى and commands that the highest name be glorified rather than treated as the best gaming arrow.
الَّذِي خَلَقَ فَسَوَّى makes creation an act of fitting and ordering; it identifies what the Lord Most High of 87:1 does and grounds the source's measured خَلَقَ.
وَالَّذِي قَدَّرَ فَهَدَى joins apportioning to guidance in one divine act, directly explaining why 92 makes both the measured share and guidance God's rather than the lot's.
The buyer of magic has مَا لَهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ مِنْ خَلَاقٍ; the source's dictionary form “share” becomes the loss incurred by a chosen exchange.

فَاسْتَمْتَعُوا بِخَلَاقِهِمْ uses خَلَاق for the worldly portion earlier peoples consumed; the ayah then likens later people to them, showing an allotted share spent away rather than retained for the last.
This continuation of 5:90 names الْخَمْرِ وَالْمَيْسِرِ again and shows the game's actual distribution—enmity, hatred, and diversion from remembrance and prayer—rather than beneficial provision.

أُولَئِكَ لَهُمْ نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا gives the two-world petitioners a share from what they earned; نَصِيب is the source's dictionary gloss for خَلَاق and replaces lucky allotment with accountable acquisition, answering 2:200.
The seeker of the worldly harvest receives some of it yet has وَمَا لَهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ مِن نَّصِيبٍ; this restates the image's first-versus-last share in agricultural rather than gaming terms.
أَمْ لَهُمْ نَصِيبٌ مِّنَ الْمُلْكِ joins “share” and “dominion” exactly; their refusal to give people even a speck shows why possessing a portion does not make one its generous lord.
The one to whom the dominion belongs خَلَقَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ فَقَدَّرَهُ تَقْدِيرًا; ownership, creation, and exact apportionment meet in the same sentence, as the source's خَلَقَ wordplay proposes.
إِنَّا كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْنَاهُ بِقَدَرٍ directly binds creation to measure, turning “cut to measure before division” into a claim about every created thing.
لِلَّهِ مُلْكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ is followed by creation at will and the gift of females or males; dominion, creating the two sexes, and allotting a gift all belong to one giver.
God pairs males and females or makes whom He wills barren; continuing 42:49, this ayah makes the human “share” of offspring a knowledgeable divine allotment rather than a claim of ownership.
The ayah joins creation from one soul and its mate, repeated creation in wombs, رَبُّكُمْ, and لَهُ الْمُلْكُ; it gathers the source's creator, pair, Lord, and owner into one scene.
مِن نُّطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُ فَقَدَّرَهُ states human creation and apportionment together, giving the source's “measured before cutting” sense a bodily referent.
وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى is a divine promise of being eased toward ease; beside 87:1–3 it makes yusr the Creator's guided provision, not the result of a gaming draw.
وَمَن يَتَّقِ اللَّهَ يَجْعَل لَّهُ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ يُسْرًا repeats 92's precise moral relation: reverence is followed by God-given ease.
Each person spends according to capacity and only from what God has given; سَيَجْعَلُ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا unites apportioned provision, giving, and promised ease.

A gift intended to grow فِي أَمْوَالِ النَّاسِ does not grow with God, whereas zakat تُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَ اللَّهِ does; wealth, purification, and seeking God's face reproduce 92:18–20 while excluding a human return.
وَمَا تُنفِقُونَ إِلَّا ابْتِغَاءَ وَجْهِ اللَّهِ is the closest formulation of the giver's sole purpose in 92:20 and locates repayment of the gift with God.
They give food despite loving it to the needy, orphan, and captive; this supplies the costly act whose motive is stated in 76:9 and parallels giving one's wealth to purify oneself.
إِنَّمَا نُطْعِمُكُمْ لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ and seeking neither recompense nor thanks directly unfold 92:19–20's gift made with no human favor to repay.
خُذْ مِنْ أَمْوَالِهِمْ صَدَقَةً تُطَهِّرُهُمْ وَتُزَكِّيهِم ties wealth given away to purification, making explicit the relation compressed in 92:18.
مَا أَغْنَى عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ is an almost verbal twin of 92:11: acquired wealth gives no protection at the decisive fall.
مَا أَغْنَى عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ is the condemned person's own recognition that “my wealth” did not avail, exposing the limit of grammatical possession.
يَوْمَ لَا يَنفَعُ مَالٌ وَلَا بَنُونَ states the final boundary of wealth's usefulness that 92:11 stages as the owner's fall.
وَآتُوهُم مِّن مَّالِ اللَّهِ الَّذِي آتَاكُمْ calls the property being transferred “God's wealth” even while it is in human hands, exactly clarifying delegated ownership.
The question “why do you not spend?” is grounded in وَلِلَّهِ مِيرَاثُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ, so refusing a gift cannot prevent the owner from inheriting it.
Those called to spend include one who withholds, but فَإِنَّمَا يَبْخَلُ عَن نَّفْسِهِ and اللَّهُ الْغَنِيُّ expose stinginess as self-harm before the true, need-free owner.

The sacrificial camels are made God's rites, then their meat is eaten and shared with the contented and the asker; this is the source's slaughtered-camel distribution transformed from gambling into worship and provision.
Neither the camel's meat nor blood reaches God, but piety does; continuing 22:36, it makes the moral intention—not the size of a drawn portion—the value of the division.
الْمَاءَ قِسْمَةٌ بَيْنَهُمْ makes water an apportioned share between the people and the she-camel announced in 54:27, a divinely set turn rather than a random prize.
The she-camel has a drink-share and the people have a drink-share on a known day; an animal and a precisely measured portion meet without gaming arrows.
نَاقَةَ اللَّهِ وَسُقْيَاهَا names both God's she-camel and her allotted drink, placing ownership and share under God's sign before the people destroy it.
مَالِكَ الْمُلْكِ gives dominion and removes it, exalts and abases; the true owner actively allots rank and property rather than surrendering them to chance.

وَرَبُّكَ يَخْلُقُ مَا يَشَاءُ وَيَخْتَارُ ... مَا كَانَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ says creation and selection belong to the Lord and denies creatures the final choice, the clearest reversal of the deciding lot.
مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ اللَّهِ بَاقٍ uses “with/at” as possession and sets perishing human holdings against what remains with God.
The one who wants the immediate world receives only what God wills and for whom He wills; desire does not itself determine the worldly allotment.
The one who desires the hereafter, believes, and strives for it has that striving appreciated; continuing 17:18, the final portion follows directed effort rather than a fortunate draw.
كُلًّا نُّمِدُّ ... مِنْ عَطَاءِ رَبِّكَ says both groups are extended from the Lord's gift, identifying the common provider behind their different aims in 17:18–19.
Worldly gradations are surpassed by the hereafter's greater degrees; this completes 17:18–20 by distinguishing a present allotment from the higher final one.
وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَى assigns a person what he strives for, replacing wished-for or randomly drawn possession with accountable effort.
His striving will be seen; this continues 53:39 and makes the basis of the coming allotment manifest rather than hidden in a chance draw.
ثُمَّ يُجْزَاهُ الْجَزَاءَ الْأَوْفَى promises the fullest repayment for the seen striving, giving “a favor repaid” its just divine rather than human setting.
وَأَنَّ إِلَى رَبِّكَ الْمُنتَهَى closes 53:39–41 at the Lord, so the final accounting and destination return to the owner named in the source.
The wealthy claim نَحْنُ أَكْثَرُ أَمْوَالًا وَأَوْلَادًا and infer they will not be punished; the scene exposes the false conversion of a large worldly share into final security.
The Lord expands and restricts provision for whom He wills; answering the boast in 34:35, this identifies wealth as apportioned provision, not proof of its holder's rank.
وَمَا أَمْوَالُكُمْ وَلَا أَوْلَادُكُم بِالَّتِي تُقَرِّبُكُمْ عِندَنَا denies that possessions bring their owners near; faith and righteous action, not the share held, determine doubled recompense.
The Lord who expands and restricts provision replaces whatever is spent and is the best provider, joining measured allotment to voluntary giving.
A person whose Lord honors and favors him says “my Lord has honored me”; the ayah stages human interpretation of a divinely given share.
When the Lord measures his provision, the person says he has been humiliated; قَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ exposes the mistake of treating a smaller allotment as a verdict on worth.
كَلَّا answers both readings in 89:15–16 and points instead to failure to honor the orphan, shifting worth from what one receives to how one gives.
Failure to urge feeding the poor continues the correction of 89:15–17: moral rank lies in sharing provision, not in the amount allotted.
أَهُمْ يَقْسِمُونَ رَحْمَتَ رَبِّكَ challenges human division, while نَحْنُ قَسَمْنَا بَيْنَهُم مَّعِيشَتَهُمْ assigns worldly livelihoods and ranks to the Lord.
Divine treasuries hold every thing and it descends only بِقَدَرٍ مَّعْلُومٍ; the human portion is a measured release from what remains with its owner.
Men and women each have نَصِيبٌ مَّفْرُوضٌ from inherited property; this is a legally fixed share, sharply distinct from the camel portion won by an arrow.
God Himself assigns male and female inheritance portions and calls them فَرِيضَةً مِّنَ اللَّهِ; the created pair of 92:3 thus receives measured property shares from the owner.
The spouse and sibling shares continue God's detailed apportionment in 4:11, showing property cut into known obligations rather than lucky portions.
The idolaters manufacture one share for God and one for their partners from crops and cattle; the ayah condemns creatures acting as owners who allot God's provision by claim.
They assign لِمَا لَا يَعْلَمُونَ نَصِيبًا مِّمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ; the false religious share is carved from provision whose giver is God.
Seek the last abode with what God has given while not forgetting نَصِيبَكَ مِنَ الدُّنْيَا and doing good as He did good to you; the two shares are ordered through received wealth and renewed giving.
Do not covet what God gave some over others; men and women each have a share of what they earned and are told to ask God, locating both earning and bounty outside envious chance.
Wealth and children are the adornment of nearer life, while lasting good deeds are better عِندَ رَبِّكَ; the verse contrasts held property with what remains at the Lord.
Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment, whereas مَا عِندَ اللَّهِ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَى; the “with” relation distinguishes temporary custody from lasting possession.
Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment, and what is عِندَ اللَّهِ is better and more lasting for believers who trust their Lord; the ayah repeats the image's ownership boundary.
Righteousness includes giving wealth despite loving it and joins that act to belief and reverence; this closely matches 92's sequence of giving, taqwa, and affirming the best.
لَن تَنَالُوا الْبِرَّ حَتَّى تُنفِقُوا مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ makes surrender of valued property the path to goodness and says God knows every expenditure.
Hear, obey, and spend for your own good; whoever is guarded from the self's stinginess prospers, directly rendering 92's giver-and-miser division.
They prefer others over themselves despite need, and protection from the self's stinginess marks success; this is a social distribution governed by generosity instead of chance.
وَلَا تَمْنُن تَسْتَكْثِرُ forbids giving in order to obtain more, setting a boundary around the source's gift for which no human favor is being repaid.
Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminder or injury receive their reward with their Lord; the giver relinquishes both property and a claim over the recipient.
Charity nullified by reminder, injury, or display reverses 92:19–20's gift free of human leverage and directed only to the Lord's face.
Spending ابْتِغَاءَ مَرْضَاتِ اللَّهِ makes divine pleasure the giver's aim and turns the amount given into fruit rather than a gaming return.
وَفِي أَمْوَالِهِمْ حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ says that within “their wealth” is a known, measured right, limiting the owner's claim from inside the possession itself.
The known right in 70:24 belongs to the asker and deprived, identifying the recipients whose portion the apparent owner must release.
وَفِي أَمْوَالِهِمْ حَقٌّ لِّلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ likewise locates another person's due within their wealth, making ownership carry an obligation to share.
If people possessed the treasuries of the Lord's mercy, they would withhold for fear of spending; the hypothetical makes miserliness the decisive difference between human and divine ownership.
Some covenant that if God gives from His bounty they will give charity; the promised gift is explicitly conditional on first receiving an allotment from God.
When God gives them from His bounty, they withhold and turn away; this continuation makes received provision reveal the same miserly path as 92:8 and 92:16.
Those who are stingy, urge stinginess, and hide what God gave from His bounty treat allotted provision as private mastery rather than a trust to be shared.
Those who are stingy and command stinginess are answered that God is the self-sufficient, praiseworthy one; the holder's refusal cannot make him the true owner.
أَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أَبْغِي رَبًّا وَهُوَ رَبُّ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ voices the source dictionary's “Lord of every thing,” then makes each soul answer for what it earns.
رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ directly joins the Lord to creating, the same link the source draws between 92:20 and 92:3.
أَن رَّآهُ اسْتَغْنَى gives self-sufficiency as the reason the human transgresses, exposing the stance of the miser who treats wealth as enough.
إِنَّ إِلَى رَبِّكَ الرُّجْعَى answers the imagined self-sufficiency of 96:7 with return to the Lord, where human possession ends.
To God belongs all in heavens and earth so that evil and good may be repaid by their deeds; ownership and just recompense replace fortune as the basis of the final share.
God created cattle by His own making and فَهُمْ لَهَا مَالِكُونَ; the ayah grants real human ownership inside a prior divine act of creation.
لِّمَنِ الْمُلْكُ الْيَوْمَ ... لِلَّهِ answers the final day's ownership question explicitly, when no human claim or drawn share remains.
A soul possesses nothing for another soul on that day and الْأَمْرُ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِّلَّهِ; final ownership and disposal are exclusively God's.

فَسَاهَمَ فَكَانَ مِنَ الْمُدْحَضِينَ stages an actual lot on the ship; unlike meysir, it allocates an emergency burden rather than distributing a slaughtered prize, marking the boundary between lot-casting and gambling.
The guardians cast their pens to decide who would care for Mary; this is a noncommercial lot for responsibility, a concrete counter-scene to arrows drawn for shares of meat.
Pharaoh says أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَى, seizing the exact joined titles “Lord” and “highest” for himself; his claim is the human counterfeit of 92:20.
God seizes the false highest lord as a lesson of الْآخِرَةِ وَالْأُولَى; continuing 79:24, both temporal realms become the scope of judgment rather than Pharaoh's ownership.
Israel objects to Saul's kingship because he lacks abundant wealth, but the prophet says God chose him and gives His dominion to whom He wills; divine selection overturns wealth-based entitlement.
Final outcome is not بِأَمَانِيِّكُمْ nor the wishes of another community but follows deeds; this supplies the accountability boundary behind 53:24's denial that a person owns whatever he wishes.
بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا diagnoses preference for the nearer life, the choice that turns a present share into loss of the last.
وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَى answers 87:16 and gives the lasting reason not to mistake the nearer allotment for the greater possession.
كَلَّا بَلْ تُحِبُّونَ الْعَاجِلَةَ names love of the immediate world as the stance opposed to the source's ownership of both first and last.
وَتَذَرُونَ الْآخِرَةَ completes 75:20 by showing that preference is an abandonment of the final share, not merely enjoyment of a present one.
Do they think the wealth and sons supplied to them prove something about their standing? The question isolates the mistaken inference from a large worldly allotment.
نُسَارِعُ لَهُمْ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ rejects the inference posed in 23:55; abundant provision is not necessarily the final good its holder imagines.
The one who جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ treats wealth as something accumulated and counted, the possessive attitude tested by 92:11.
يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ states the hoarder's false conclusion; wealth cannot confer permanence and instead fails exactly where the final owner matters.
When relatives, orphans, and the poor attend the division, the heirs are told to provide for them from it; this places voluntary giving at the edge of a formally allotted estate.
A person who intercedes for good or evil has a نَصِيب or كِفْل from it; the source's “share” becomes a moral consequence generated by participation rather than chance.
يَنَالُهُمْ نَصِيبُهُم مِّنَ الْكِتَابِ portrays a decreed portion reaching wrongdoers before death; it is a less material instance of an allotted share arriving from a prior measure.
وَإِنَّا لَمُوَفُّوهُمْ نَصِيبَهُمْ غَيْرَ مَنقُوصٍ promises the idolaters their undiminished portion, making the final allotment exact even when it is punishment.
The spoils ayah fixes named fractions and recipients and first says أَنَّ لِلَّهِ خُمُسَهُ; gained property is divided under divine title rather than by a lucky arrow.
God-directed distribution of recovered property is designed كَيْ لَا يَكُونَ دُولَةً بَيْنَ الْأَغْنِيَاءِ, so a communal share does not circulate only among wealthy possessors.
لَن تُغْنِيَ عَنْهُمْ أَمْوَالُهُمْ ... مِنَ اللَّهِ شَيْئًا repeats the limit on wealth's power and places its owners at the fire, though it lacks the source's falling image.
The same formula says the disbelievers' wealth and children will not avail against God at all; it is a repeated Quranic boundary on apparent possession.
Neither wealth nor children avail against God, and their owners become companions of the fire; this connects the failed property of 92:11 to its warned fire.
فَجَعَلَ مِنْهُ الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنثَى repeats the male-female pair of 92:3 in a context where prior ayat describe creating and proportioning, supporting creation as measured formation.
The garden owners agree that no poor person will enter upon them that day; the harvest is treated as an exclusive private share and withheld before it is even gathered.
After the garden is destroyed they say بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ; those who planned to deprive the poor in 68:24 discover that their own expected portion was never secured.
عَسَى رَبُّنَا أَن يُبْدِلَنَا خَيْرًا مِّنْهَا ends the garden scene by returning replacement property to the Lord's allotment, though it remains a hope rather than a promise.
